paras: The masked-band attack on Wallace Thompson's home was a night raid in late August 1885 on a farm about four miles from Columbus, Georgia, in Lee County, Alabama. Masked men broke into Thompson's house, chased him into the dark and whipped several Black people on his place to make them tell where he had gone. Thompson sold his property and fled across the river to Georgia; the only known report rests on his own account.

According to the account Thompson gave in Columbus on Friday, a "mob of masked men" surrounded his home about midnight on Wednesday night and broke open the door and window. Hearing the attack begin, he escaped through a back window in his night clothes, and the attackers chased him about a quarter of a mile before giving up. Thompson said the band then whipped "several negroes on his place to force them to tell his whereabouts"; the paper gave neither their names nor their number.
Thompson said it was the second time a party had come to his house at night, and he claimed not to know the reason for either visit.

Thompson had not gone home since the attack, and he said he had sold everything he owned in Lee County on Friday and never expected to cross into Alabama again. He said he knew the names of two of the party and would make them public, but no later report naming them, or of any arrest, was found.

The episode appears only as one paragraph in the Savannah Morning News of 30 August 1885, in its "Georgia and Florida" column of short items. The column's headline deck described "An Alabama[ian] Driven from Home by Vigilant[e]s" who "Seeks Refuge in Georgia," presenting Thompson rather than the people who were whipped as the subject of the story. The item attributed each detail to Thompson ("he says," "he also states"), gave no race for him or for his attackers, and used "negroes" only for the people who were whipped.
No Black-press coverage of the attack and no report from a Columbus or Lee County paper were found.

accounts.label: Thompson's statement at Columbus
accounts.gist: Masked men surrounded his house at midnight, broke in and chased him a quarter of a mile after he escaped through a back window. They whipped several Black people on his place to learn where he had gone. It was their second visit, and he did not know why they came.

framing.detail: A short item in a regional news-in-brief column. It relays Thompson's account as his report ('he says', 'he also states') without comment and calls the attackers 'Vigilant[e]s' in the headline deck.

record_check.dossier: Wallace Thompson was driven out, and several unnamed 'negroes' on his place were whipped. The whipped people are the only victims the paper identifies as Black.
The paper does not give Thompson's race. The people who were whipped are called 'negroes'.
'Several' Black people were whipped; no number is given.
Supported. Driving Thompson from his home should be added: he sold out and left Alabama.
Rural, about four miles from Columbus, Ga., on the Alabama side of the river

record_check.record: ...whipped several negroes on his place to force them to reveal his whereabouts.
record_check.dossier: Accurate, but every detail is Thompson's own account. The record also leaves out that this was the second visit and that he sold his property and left Alabama.
